scenario.name: Dental assistant
scenario.idea: A tool that listens to dentist-patient visits, writes clinical notes and suggests diagnoses.
expected: Clinical hallucination / medical device oversight (FDA; KB gap)

advisor.summary: This tool records dentist-patient conversations, sends health audio and records to a third-party AI, and suggests diagnoses to clinicians, so the main risks are sensitive health data, possible medical-device oversight, and patient harm from wrong output. Several risks depend on facts not yet given, such as which states you serve, whether your customers are covered by health privacy rules, and how the diagnostic suggestions are presented.

risks.severityWhy: High: sensitive health data and audio of patients, with no safeguards described.
risks.title: Patient health information may trigger HIPAA obligations
risks.why: Dental practices may be HIPAA covered entities, which could make you a business associate when you process their audio and records. That may affect contracts, permitted uses of the data, and whether you can use it for model improvement.
risks.fix: Confirm with each customer whether HIPAA applies. Prepare a standard business associate agreement. Collect only the audio and record fields needed for notes. Turn off any use of patient data for your own model training by default. Set a configurable retention period and a deletion workflow for audio.

risks.severityWhy: High: suggested diagnoses could cause direct harm to patients and could affect whether you can launch.
risks.title: Diagnosis suggestions may be regulated as medical device software
risks.why: Software that suggests diagnoses to clinicians may fall under FDA oversight depending on its function and on whether clinicians can independently review the basis for the suggestions. 'Informs a human' alone may not settle this.
risks.fix: Write down the intended use. Show the transcript evidence behind each suggestion so the clinician can verify it. Label suggestions as non-final. Consider shipping note-writing first and gating the diagnosis feature until you have a regulatory assessment.

risks.severityWhy: High: recording private conversations about patients, with no consent mechanism described, could block launch in some states.
risks.title: Recording consent varies by state
risks.why: Recording visits may be subject to state rules on recording conversations, and some states may require all parties to consent. None of the listed sources address this, so it needs legal review.
risks.fix: Build a consent step into the product: a patient-facing notice or script, a clinic-side consent log, and a visible recording indicator. Add an easy way to pause or stop recording and to run a visit without AI. Set consent defaults by state once your target states are known.

risks.severityWhy: High: sensitive health data and audio flow to a third-party API, and no safeguards are described.
risks.title: Third-party AI API could expose patient data
risks.why: Sending audio and records to an outside model provider creates risks of data leakage, unwanted retention or training on the data, and prompt injection through spoken or record content. Your vendor's terms may also affect your HIPAA position.
risks.fix: Use a vendor that will sign a business associate agreement, with zero-retention and no-training terms. Encrypt data in transit and at rest. Strip direct identifiers before sending when possible. Add access controls and audit logs. Test for prompt injection and keep model outputs from triggering actions automatically.

risks.severityWhy: Medium: plausible patient-safety harm that needs mitigation before scaling, and the clinician review step reduces the immediate risk.
risks.title: Made-up or wrong notes and diagnoses entering the record
risks.why: Generative models can invent findings or miss them. Busy clinicians may over-trust the output, and errors can carry into the patient's record and later care.
risks.fix: Require clinician review and sign-off before any note is saved. Highlight AI-inserted diagnoses and uncertain passages. Link each statement to the transcript segment it came from. Track correction rates and provide an in-app error reporting button.

risks.severityWhy: Medium: plausibly applies, and uneven accuracy needs testing and mitigation before wider release.
risks.title: Uneven transcription and diagnostic accuracy across patient groups
risks.why: Speech recognition can perform worse for some accents, languages, speech patterns, and noisy rooms. Diagnostic suggestions may also reflect gaps in training data, which could mean worse notes or missed findings for some patients.
risks.fix: Test accuracy by accent, language, age, and audio conditions before release. Set minimum performance thresholds. Provide a language or accuracy warning when confidence is low. Monitor error rates by group after launch and keep an incident process.

risks.severityWhy: Medium: plausibly applies, and marketing and data-handling claims need review before scaling sales.
risks.title: Accuracy and privacy claims could be seen as deceptive
risks.why: Claims such as 'accurate', 'HIPAA-compliant', 'secure', or 'doesn't store audio' may be scrutinized if they overstate what the product does or what happens to the data.
risks.fix: Keep a claims log that ties each marketing and sales statement to test results or technical facts. Avoid 'compliant' or 'certified' wording unless it has been verified. Make sure your privacy policy matches the real data flows, including the AI vendor.

risks.severityWhy: Medium: breach and health-privacy rules plausibly apply, but your target states are not stated.
risks.title: State-specific breach and health data rules are unmapped
risks.why: 'Other US states' may include states with their own breach-notice, health-data, or consumer-privacy rules. None of the listed sources cover them.
risks.fix: List the states you will sell into. Write an incident response plan with contact points and customer notification steps. Keep an inventory of where audio, transcripts, and notes are stored. Add contract terms for breach notice with your customers and your AI vendor.

askLawyer: Would we be a HIPAA business associate for our dental customers, and what contracts do we need with them and with our AI vendor?
Do our diagnosis suggestions need an FDA assessment, and how should we scope or present them to stay within a lower-risk category?
Which recording-consent and health-privacy rules apply in the states where we plan to sell, and how should consent be captured?

plain.text:
# Risk Assessment: AI Dental Scribe and Diagnosis Suggestion Tool

## Highest-priority risks

### 1. Diagnosis suggestions may make this a regulated medical device
- Software that suggests diagnoses can fall under FDA oversight as Software as a Medical Device. The Clinical Decision Support exemption is narrow, and it requires that the clinician can independently review the basis for each recommendation. Black-box suggestions derived from audio or images may not qualify.
- Note-taking alone is low-risk from an FDA perspective. Adding diagnosis moves you into a much higher regulatory tier.
- **Consider:** launching scribe-only first, getting a regulatory opinion before shipping diagnostic features, and framing suggestions as "items to consider" with visible supporting evidence (e.g., the transcript segment).

### 2. Recording consent and state law
- Several states require **all-party consent** to record (e.g., CA, FL, IL, MD, MA, PA, WA). Patients, family members, and interpreters in the room may all be captured.
- **Voiceprint and biometric laws** (e.g., Illinois BIPA, Texas, Washington) can apply if your system does speaker identification.
- Newer state health-data and AI laws (e.g., Washington's My Health My Data Act, Colorado's AI Act, Texas and Utah AI rules) add disclosure and governance duties that vary by state.
- **Mitigation:** build a consent workflow into the product, with patient notice, a per-visit opt-out, and state-aware defaults. Don't leave this to each clinic.

### 3. HIPAA and third-party API exposure
- You'd likely be a **business associate**, and your model vendor a **subcontractor**. You need BAAs through the whole chain.
- Confirm that the vendor offers zero data retention, doesn't train on your data, and discloses its subprocessors and data locations.
- Audio is highly sensitive and can contain identifiers beyond the clinical content, such as names, addresses, and insurance details.
- Set retention limits, encryption, access controls, and breach-response plans. Decide whether you need to keep the raw audio at all.

### 4. Clinical accuracy errors
- **Hallucinations and omissions:** invented findings, or missed allergies, medications, or patient concerns.
- **Dental-specific errors:** tooth numbers, quadrants, surfaces, and periodontal charting readings are easy to mishear, and a wrong tooth number can lead to wrong-site treatment.
- **Audio conditions:** drills, suction, masks, multiple speakers, and patients who are mid-procedure and can't speak clearly.
- **Speaker attribution:** confusing what the dentist said with what the patient said (e.g., a patient-reported symptom recorded as a clinical finding).
- Audio-only diagnosis is weak, because dental diagnosis relies heavily on radiographs, probing, and exam findings that may never be spoken aloud.

### 5. Automation bias and the "human in the loop" problem
- A busy dentist may skim and sign AI notes, and may anchor on a suggested diagnosis. The human is only a real safeguard if review is easy and actually happens.
- **Mitigation:** show source-linked evidence, highlight low-confidence items, make edits easy, and track how often notes are edited versus accepted unchanged. Very low edit rates are a warning sign.

## Significant risks

### 6. Billing and fraud exposure
- If suggested diagnoses or notes drive procedure codes, you could inadvertently encourage upcoding or documentation that supports unnecessary treatment. This creates False Claims Act and insurer audit risk for your customers, and reputational risk for you.
- Audit your suggestions for systematic bias toward higher-revenue treatments.

### 7. Liability allocation
- Who is responsible when a note error or suggestion contributes to patient harm? Expect disputes among the clinic, you, and your model vendor.
- You'll need clear contracts, disclaimers that match actual product behavior, indemnification terms, and professional/tech E&O and cyber insurance.
- AI-generated notes are part of the legal record and can be discoverable.

### 8. Bias and performance disparities
- Speech recognition often performs worse for some accents, dialects, and non-native speakers, as well as for children and patients with speech impairments.
- Interpreter-mediated visits and multilingual visits are especially error-prone.
- Test performance across demographic groups and report it, rather than relying on aggregate accuracy.

### 9. Dependence on a third-party model
- Model updates can silently change output quality, so you'll need regression testing against a clinical test set.
- Deprecations, outages, rate limits, and price changes can hit your margins and uptime.
- Vendor terms may change on data use. Consider a fallback provider or an abstraction layer.
- Your differentiation is thin if you only wrap a general API, because competitors can replicate it quickly.

## Business and adoption risks
- **Integration:** clinics rely on practice management and imaging systems (e.g., Dentrix, Eaglesoft, Open Dental). Without tight integration, adoption stalls.
- **Crowded market:** established dental AI players and general medical scribes are already moving in.
- **Patient trust:** some patients will resist being recorded, and some may speak less candidly.
- **Workflow fit:** dental visits are procedural and often involve little conversation, so the scribe may capture less useful content than in a medical office visit.

## Suggested risk-reduction roadmap
1. **Start with scribe-only** and add diagnostic suggestions later, after regulatory review and validation.
2. **Get a regulatory and privacy legal review** covering FDA, HIPAA, and state recording, biometric, and AI laws.
3. **Lock down the vendor setup:** BAA, zero retention, no training on your data, and subprocessor transparency.
4. **Design review into the workflow:** require clinician sign-off, with source-linked evidence and flagged uncertainty.
5. **Build a dental-specific evaluation set** covering tooth numbering, noise, accents, and multi-speaker audio, and run it on every model change.
6. **Pilot with a few friendly clinics** and track error rates, edit rates, and near misses.
7. **Monitor continuously** for drift, bias, and billing-pattern anomalies.

If you tell me which states you're targeting and whether diagnosis suggestions use only audio or also images and records, I can narrow this down to the most relevant legal and technical risks.
